Join us for a hands-on floral design experience focused on creating a beautiful centerpiece for your Thanksgiving holiday. In this intimate workshop, guests will learn foundational bouquet-making techniques using locally sourced fall blooms and foliage.What to expect:
*   Learn the basics of flower care, sustainable mechanics, and design techniques to create your own stunning centerpiece  
*   Indulge in our signature charcuterie spread and sip on delightful sips  
*   Take home your very own gorgeous floral creation, along with new skills and memories to cherish
This floral design class is perfect for those curious about the art of flower arranging, a creative day out, or hosts looking to make a unique piece for their Thanksgiving table!

# Fall Floral Arranging Workshop
**Thursday, November 5 | 6:30 PM to 8:00 PM**
Join us at the MARKET HOUSE for a cozy and creative evening of fall floral arranging! Learn the art of creating a beautiful seasonal arrangement using fresh autumn blooms, rich colors, and natural textures.
Whether you're a flower enthusiast or simply looking for a fun evening with friends, this hands-on workshop is the perfect way to get creative, enjoy some light bites, and welcome the season.
**Your ticket includes:**
*   A curated selection of fresh seasonal flowers

*   A vessel and all arranging supplies

*   Guided floral arranging instruction

*   Light bites and refreshments

*   Your very own arrangement to take home!
**BYOB:** Feel free to bring your favorite wine, bubbly, or beverage to sip while you create! Alcoholic beverages are for guests ages 21 and over.
**Limited to 15 guests** for an intimate, personalized experience. Advance registration is required.
No experience necessary. Just bring yourself and a little creativity!

**Thursday, November 5 | 6:30 PM to 8:00 PM**
Join us at the MARKET HOUSE for a cozy and creative evening of fall floral arranging! Learn the art of creating a beautiful seasonal arrangement using fresh autumn blooms, rich colors, and natural textures.
Whether you're a flower enthusiast or simply looking for a fun evening with friends, this hands-on workshop is the perfect way to get creative, enjoy some light bites, and welcome the season.
**Your ticket includes:**
*   A curated selection of fresh seasonal flowers

*   A vessel and all arranging supplies

*   Guided floral arranging instruction

*   Light bites and refreshments

*   Your very own arrangement to take home!

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Maque Café
Part of a small chain of cozy bakeries, the here pastries are serviceable. But dine at a table for the full cafe menu, which includes huevos rancheros served with warm, soupy black beans.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 209, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 2489 5695](tel:525524895695)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Turix
One of the best taquerias in the city looks completely out of place just steps from DF’s Louis Vuitton, but it’s one of the main reasons food enthusiasts will visit this part of town (if they’re not staying nearby already). Get anything with the house _cochinita pibil_, a style of slow-roasted pork from the Yucatán.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 212, Miguel Hidalgo, Distrito Federa, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 6449](tel:525552806449)

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Pujol
Enrique Olvera’s fine dining restaurant is world-famous for a reason: it serves really fantastic food. Get a little dressed up for the elegant dinnertime tasting menu, or try for a more casual lunch, provided you plan ahead and score a reservation. Try calling at the last minute for late afternoon tables, which are sometimes easier to get than prime times.
Loved it Want to try
*   Francisco Petrarca 254, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11570, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5545 4111](tel:525555454111)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Quintonil
Chef Jorge Vallejo and his wife Alejandra Flores are behind this, Mexico City’s current fine dining mecca. That Vallejo trained under Olvera at Pujol, and has something to prove, is something you might hear whispered in the dining room. So far, the critics and the people love it. Consider the a la carte menu for lunch.
Loved it Want to try
*   Newton 55, Polanco, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 2680](tel:525552802680)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Dulce Patria
Chef Martha Ortiz just snagged a spot on the new Top Chef Mexico; her dramatic flair and feminist ideals will likely be a welcome addition to this franchise of the Bravo show. Her restaurant draws an unsurprisingly hip clientele, and the dining room’s decoration — scarlet, white, and fuchsia — hints at the dishes to come. Ortiz’s food is romantic, but bold and completely unexpected.
Loved it Want to try
*   Anatole France 100, Mexico City, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 3300 3999](tel:525533003999)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Jules Basement
You’ll never find this place unless someone tells you where it is. Hidden behind what looks like the door to a walk-in cooler inside a basic cantina is one of this part of town’s coolest bars. It’s not new, but the speakeasy-style is fun and the drinks are grand.
Loved it Want to try
*   Julio Verne, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Amado
What could easily have been an overwrought and overly sweet hotel bakery inside the Hyatt Regency is, happily, a fine _pastelería_ and _panadería_. It’s comfortable, serves excellent coffee, and displays dozens of flavorful, nuanced baked goods that borrow heavily from European technique.
Loved it Want to try
*   Campos Eliseos 204, Mexico, Mexico

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Chapulín
This restaurant inside the Hotel Intercontinental pays homage to Mexico’s indigenous cuisine but also offers excellent modern standards, including tacos, shellfish from Baja, and rice and beans. The service is good and the prices are fair, especially considering the location.

Title: Shopping for the Best in Mexico City — GOOD FOOD MEXICO
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
_Updated June, 2017_
I take a brief pause from my usual feast or blast review column to fill do-it-yourselfers in on my favorite sources for great products, both foreign and national. Mexico City food shopping will not disappoint the most discerning gourmand.
**MERCADO SAN JUAN** Calle Ernesto Pugibet, centro Metro Salto de Agua – walk up Calle Lopez and turn left at Delicias (or down Lopez if you are coming from the Alameda – you will see the enormous Telmex tower which is across the street view map
The market is, in theory, open daily until around 5 p.m. but some vendors start packing up earlier – there is free parking for customers next door.
This renowned market has existed in some form since colonial times. Chefs and home cooks alike frequent its aisles in search of the perfect duck, cabrito, or lobster. Exotic fresh produce and fruits are offered as are artisan national and imported cheeses: go to **Gastronomica San Juan**, stall no.162,and its neighbor **La Jersey** – they will let you sample. The nationally produced and excellent goat, cow and sheep cheese, many from the state of Queretaro are much cheaper than the imported ones. These stands, as well as **La Catalana** offer good cold cuts as well.
In the seafood area mussels, clams oysters and calamares (they will clean them on request) are often available fresh as are unusual varieties of fish, fresh tuna and amazing big shrimp either in or out of the shell. Spaniards eyes will pop when they see the hideous but delicious percebes at a fraction of the price of the old country.

In the meat section, you’ll have to stomach the piles of sacrificed kid goat and bunny corpses. Chef and food consultant Stan swears by stands 44-46 who sell veal scaloppini and ossobuco ready to cook. Nearby stands stock lamb, both New Zealand and national (which is more like mutton but good for Indian or Moroccan stews), but it is often frozen; on Fridays and Saturdays they are more likely to have thawed meat which can then be cut or ground to order. You could pick up an armadillo as well if your soiree has a pre-Hispanic theme. More tempting are fresh farm turkeys (don’t worry, they’ll remove the head and feet for you) packaged ducks, and, occasionally, free range local ducks which will produce a knockout Peking roast or á l’orange.
Several surprisingly well stocked Asian vegetable stands, the only ones in the whole country, cater to the growing population of Asian immigrants as well as people like me who want to buy bitter melon, long beans, okra, baby bok choy or pea shoots.
The ‘gourmet’ produce stands, meanwhile, offer such hard to get greenies as crinkly kale and Savoy cabbage, tiny _haricot vertes_ or yellow wax beans, celeriac, tiny peas, shelled favas and sweet potatoes. One lady has fresh herbs such as dill, tarragon and real Italian basil (not the off smelling Mexican variety, which just won’t do for Italian cooking, although it works well as a substitute for Thai basil). And, of course, there’s Doña Guadalupe, to the left as you enter, who in season, sells an amazing variety of fresh wild mushrooms, including cultivated local porcini. I always see French people at this stand madly stashing chanterelles, giroles and morels, happy to be paying 80 pesos instead of 80 euros. Dried versions are available all year around and make good gifts.
**EL MOLINERO PROGRESO** Aranda 26, centro Open Monday - Saturday 8 a.m.- 8 p.m. View mapThis deceptively small shop sells every spice and grain under the sun. You can get whatever you need to make Indian, Moroccan, Persian, Thai or Russian dishes. As well as Mexican.

**CENTRO GOURMET** Prol. Moliere 495, at (Lago Andromaco and Rio San Joachin) Polanco View mapTel. 5254-3645 This enormous store has a good selection of cookware, knives appliances etc. as well as some baking ingredients like hard to find bread and rye flours.
**ASIAN FUSION:**
**MIKASA** San Luís Potosí 173, Colonia Roma Tel. 5574-4859 Open Monday – Saturday 10-7, Sunday until 6. View mapThis excellent Japanese supermarket stocks other Asian ingredients as well, like Chinese sauces, as well as some fresh produce, meat and tofu. They have freshly made bento boxes and a few tables outside so you can have a pleasant, inexpensive and authentic lunch while you’re shopping. On weekends, the front patio turns into a popular BBQ. Good fish and rice cakes are served sizzling off the coals, although recently I have noticed a disturbing preponderance of Argentine sausages and arrachera, due, I suppose, to popular demand of the ‘gaijin’ customers.
**SUPER ORIENTAL** Division del Norte 2515 corner of Londres, (Londres, you will recall, is the ‘Frida house’ street – this place is at the other end of it, about 15 blocks away) Coyoacán Tel. 5688-2981 Open Monday – Saturday 9:30-7:30 PM, Sunday 10:30-3:30 PM View map Asian cooking supplies, kitchen utensils such as a good variety of woks –this is the best and biggest pan-asian market in the city.
**KOREAN SHOPS**Calle Hamburgo Between Florencia and Sevilla, Zona Rosa There are several Korean markets in a row selling fresh tofu, kim chi and other Korean and general Asian necessities. Numbers 214, where they make huge chunks of meaty fresh tofu, and 238, view map, are my favorites; neither have signs nor numbers, so look for the plain white doors and figure out where they are according to the other numbered buildings.
**THE MIDDLE EAST:**

**ADONIS** Hegel 205, Polanco, view map,Branch in Tecamachalco, Av. de Las Fuentes no. 49-B View map, Open daily Monday-Wednesday 1 p.m. - 12 a.m., Thursday-Saturday 1 p.m.-2 a.m., Sunday 1–7 p.m. Tel. 5531- 6940/ 5531-8081 This store, connected to a restaurant of the same name, is a good source for Middle Eastern supplies as well as basmati and Arborio rices, cous cous, olives and fabulous fattening honey desserts.
Mamma mia, it’s Italian:
**BENEPASTA** Ayuntamiento 12, view map, centro Fresa 142, Ciudad Satélite These stores sell dried pastas in many unusual shapes, as well as semolina (for making fresh pasta) and fresh ravioli. The original store is around the corner from the aforementioned Mercado San Juan.
**PARTIMAR GASTRONOMÍA ITALIANA** Rosas Moreno 32 (near Ribera San Cosme) San Rafael Tel. 5566-3544/5566-3058, view map.This large shop is located in the old working class neighborhood of San Rafael, only a few blocks from the San Cosme metro stop. It’s a good source for all kinds of packaged products, oils and vinegars, as well as cheeses and meats. They have a smart selection of reasonably priced Italian wines. Several pasta machines are for sale here too. One-day cooking classes are offered periodically – call for information.
**CENTRO GOURMET VITTORIO** Prol. Bosques de Reforma 1371, Lomas Tel. 5251-3186, view map. This is a store specializing in all kinds of fresh pasta as well as imported cheeses and gourmet products. See their website: www.vittorio.com.mx
**BOTTEGA CULINARIA**, Sonora 180, Condesa, Open Daily 9 a.m. - 11p.m., view map. This 'gourmet' shop, connected to an Italian restaurant, offers good imported and national cheeses, olives, pastas, breads, pastries and good prepared foods.

PARDON MY FRENCH::
**CHRISSON GASTRONOMÍA FRANCESA** Cuernavaca 135, corner of Campeche This French-owned shop sells their own patés and terrines and also offers catering service.
**Olivier Dekeyser** is a patissier divine. He does Belgian style cakes and pastries to order for any occasion; see his site:http://elpostrebelga.mx/
Oy, so ver do I get za pickles?:
**KURSON KOSHER** Emilio Castelar 204, Polanco, view map. This kosher market which makes more than acceptable pastrami and corned beef if you have a yen for it. But don't get too excited: it ain't Zabar's. There is a branch in the huge Tecamachalco kosher mall on Av. Fuente de Templanza.
**CITY MARKET**(see website for branch locations) is really a gussied up supermarket, but they do have particularly good meat and fish departments as well as many choices of canned and bottled goods like olive oil and vinegar. The wine selection is excellent
**Kameyama Shachuu**is the only shop in the city offering an a array of jewel-like Japanese knives. The showroom is worth a stop even if you don’t do your own sashimi. Knives for all purposes are on display from simple and relatively affordable chef knives to beautiful hand-hewn and understandably expensive examples whose purposes remain a mystery.
**Kameyama Shachu**u Av. Alvaro Obregón 230, Roma Nte. Open Wednesday – Monday 11 a.m. – 7 p.m., closed Tuesday
See also: The Condesa Tuesday Tianguis, The Polanco Saturday Tianguis

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
Don’t dismiss Mexico City’s ritziest neighborhood — it’s got a lot to offer
byDaniela Galarza
Mar 21, 2016, 1:30 PM UTC
*
It’s easy to dismiss Polanco — the Beverly Hills of Mexico City — as a skippable part of town overrun by politicos, their cronies, very wealthy locals, and very wealthy tourists. Still, it’s likely you’ll end up here for one reason or another: The city’s fanciest hotels stand in this area, and so are some of its most highly-rated restaurants. Unfortunately, they share space with American-import chain restaurants, tourist-trap quasi-European wine bars, and Starbucks. Steer clear of those options and consider these far better picks.
See guides to all of Mexico City’s greatest neighborhoods — plus everything you need to know about eating in DF, one of the best food cities in the world — in the **Eater Guide to Mexico City.**

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Maque Café
Part of a small chain of cozy bakeries, the here pastries are serviceable. But dine at a table for the full cafe menu, which includes huevos rancheros served with warm, soupy black beans.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 209, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 2489 5695](tel:525524895695)  
*   Visit Website

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Turix
One of the best taquerias in the city looks completely out of place just steps from DF’s Louis Vuitton, but it’s one of the main reasons food enthusiasts will visit this part of town (if they’re not staying nearby already). Get anything with the house _cochinita pibil_, a style of slow-roasted pork from the Yucatán.
Loved it Want to try
*   Emilio Castelar 212, Miguel Hidalgo, Distrito Federa, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 6449](tel:525552806449)
texts.6:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Pujol
Enrique Olvera’s fine dining restaurant is world-famous for a reason: it serves really fantastic food. Get a little dressed up for the elegant dinnertime tasting menu, or try for a more casual lunch, provided you plan ahead and score a reservation. Try calling at the last minute for late afternoon tables, which are sometimes easier to get than prime times.
Loved it Want to try
*   Francisco Petrarca 254, Miguel Hidalgo, Mexico City 11570, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5545 4111](tel:525555454111)  
*   Visit Website
texts.7:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Quintonil
Chef Jorge Vallejo and his wife Alejandra Flores are behind this, Mexico City’s current fine dining mecca. That Vallejo trained under Olvera at Pujol, and has something to prove, is something you might hear whispered in the dining room. So far, the critics and the people love it. Consider the a la carte menu for lunch.
Loved it Want to try
*   Newton 55, Polanco, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 5280 2680](tel:525552802680)  
*   Visit Website
texts.8:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Dulce Patria
Chef Martha Ortiz just snagged a spot on the new Top Chef Mexico; her dramatic flair and feminist ideals will likely be a welcome addition to this franchise of the Bravo show. Her restaurant draws an unsurprisingly hip clientele, and the dining room’s decoration — scarlet, white, and fuchsia — hints at the dishes to come. Ortiz’s food is romantic, but bold and completely unexpected.
Loved it Want to try
*   Anatole France 100, Mexico City, Mexico City 11560, Mexico  
*   [+52 55 3300 3999](tel:525533003999)  
*   Visit Website
texts.9:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Jules Basement
You’ll never find this place unless someone tells you where it is. Hidden behind what looks like the door to a walk-in cooler inside a basic cantina is one of this part of town’s coolest bars. It’s not new, but the speakeasy-style is fun and the drinks are grand.
Loved it Want to try
*   Julio Verne, Mexico City, Mexico City, Mexico  
*   Visit Website
texts.10:
# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## Amado
What could easily have been an overwrought and overly sweet hotel bakery inside the Hyatt Regency is, happily, a fine _pastelería_ and _panadería_. It’s comfortable, serves excellent coffee, and displays dozens of flavorful, nuanced baked goods that borrow heavily from European technique.
Loved it Want to try
*   Campos Eliseos 204, Mexico, Mexico

# Mexico City Neighborhood Guide: Polanco
## El Chapulín
This restaurant inside the Hotel Intercontinental pays homage to Mexico’s indigenous cuisine but also offers excellent modern standards, including tacos, shellfish from Baja, and rice and beans. The service is good and the prices are fair, especially considering the location.
Loved it Want to try

Source: https://www.tourme.app/mx/blog/mercado-de-san-juan-mexico-city-guide
Title: Mercado de San Juan Mexico City: A Complete Guide to the City's Gourmet Market (2026)
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
The seafood vendors are freshest before noon, and the market is far less crowded Tuesday through Friday — weekend crowds double the wait at the raw bar counters
Cheese and charcuterie vendors usually accept cards; the cooked food counters often don't — 200–300 pesos in small bills covers a full eat-through visit
Ask specifically for manchego español if you want the sheep's-milk aged version — the domestic manchego sold everywhere else in the city is a completely different product
Mexico City has roughly 300 public markets, and almost all of them follow a similar format: produce, cooked food, clothing, hardware, and household goods in rough equal measure. Mercado de San Juan, which sits on Calle Ernesto Pugibet 21 just south of the Alameda Central in Centro Histórico, took a different path. Over decades, it became the market where the city's specialty importers and gourmet food vendors concentrated — which meant the cheesemongers, the charcutiers, the exotic meat traders, and the sashimi-grade seafood suppliers who also sold to restaurants all ended up here. By the 2000s it had become the go-to source for European cheeses, Iberian charcuterie, wild mushrooms, and ingredients that simply don't exist in regular Mexican supermarkets. The result is an odd, specific place: a functioning neighborhood market with local staples on one end and imported Italian truffle and Japanese sake on the other. The building occupies a full city block, with around 200 vendor stalls organized loosely by category — cheese and charcuterie on one side, seafood and cooked food along the back, produce and specialty dry goods through the middle. It's clean, well-lit, and navigable on a first visit once you walk the full loop.
Located at Calle Ernesto Pugibet 21, Centro Histórico — nearest metro: Salto del Agua (Lines 1 and 8)
Open Monday–Saturday 9 AM–6 PM, Sunday 9 AM–5 PM
Around 200 vendor stalls in a single enclosed building

The cheese selection at San Juan is probably the best you'll find in Mexico City outside of a specialty import shop. Several stalls carry aged Spanish manchego — the real sheep's-milk version produced in La Mancha, not the mild domestic cow's-milk product sold everywhere else under the same name. You'll also find French camembert, Italian parmigiano-reggiano sold by the wedge, cave-aged Roquefort, Dutch gouda in several ages, and Spanish idiazábal. A useful exercise for first-time visitors: ask a vendor to let you taste the imported Spanish manchego next to the Mexican domestic version side by side. The difference — nutty and firm versus mild and rubbery — explains immediately why San Juan exists and why chefs make the trip from Polanco to shop here. The charcuterie stalls carry similar depth: jamón ibérico de bellota sliced to order, bresaola from Italian producers, prosciutto di Parma, and Spanish chorizo ibérico alongside excellent Mexican products including cecina from Yecapixtla (the Morelos town famous for its air-dried beef) and black chorizo from Oaxacan producers. The vendors are patient and accustomed to questions — this is one of the few markets in the city where asking for tastes before buying is normal and expected.
Get short, interactive stories that make each place easier to remember while you travel.

The seafood section runs along one side of the building, and a handful of vendors have built what amounts to a standing raw bar right between the stalls. The format is simple: fresh oysters opened to order, served with limón and hot sauce, eaten standing at a small counter. The oysters come from Baja California (Pacific oysters, briny and clean) or the Gulf of Mexico — ask the vendor which batch is freshest if both are available, since they don't restock at the same frequency. Beyond oysters, the same vendors sell tostadas de atún — raw tuna on a fried corn tostada with avocado, cucumber, and a swipe of mayo — and aguachile de camarón, raw shrimp marinated in lime juice and serrano chile until the acid 'cooks' the protein into something bright and clean-tasting with real heat at the end. The seafood vendors at San Juan source directly from suppliers who also sell to high-end restaurants, which means the quality and freshness track closely to what you'd get at a sit-down restaurant in Roma Norte for significantly less money. Expect to pay around 80–120 pesos for a serving of oysters, 60–80 for a tostada.
Pacific oysters from Baja California: briny and firm — the more reliably consistent option
Tostadas de atún: raw tuna, avocado, cucumber on a fried tostada — the best value item in the market
Aguachile: ask for the spice level before ordering — San Juan versions tend toward serious heat

The exotic meat stalls are the part of Mercado de San Juan that generates the most social media content, and they deserve both the attention and a little context. Yes, you can buy ostrich, crocodile, venison, wild boar, and occasionally lion meat at certain stalls. The vendors are licensed and the products legally sourced from registered farms — this is not a black market situation. The crocodile, which comes from regulated farms in Tabasco and Chiapas, is the most approachable option: the tail meat is lean and firm with a texture somewhere between chicken and a dense white fish, usually served as tacos with salsa verde. It's genuinely good and worth ordering once. Ostrich from Hidalgo farms is served as a steak cut — lower in fat than beef, darker in color, and mild enough that it takes a chile marinade well. The lion meat, when it appears, comes from exotic animal operations and is expensive enough that vendors price it by the gram; the flavor itself is unremarkable — mild and lean — and the price premium is entirely for the novelty. Order the crocodile. Skip the lion unless the story is the whole point for you.
Crocodile: farmed in Tabasco and Chiapas — lean tail meat served as tacos with salsa verde, genuinely worth trying
Ostrich: from Hidalgo farms — steak cut, lower fat than beef, takes seasoning well
Lion: legally sourced, overpriced for what it is — the story costs more than the flavor

San Juan is small enough to cover fully in an hour, but the most satisfying way to visit is to plan around the food counters rather than treating it as a grocery run. Start near the entrance with a slow pass through the produce section — the stacks of dried chiles, heirloom corn varieties, and specialty mushrooms (huitlacoche, morels, chanterelles) give you a sense of the market's range before you commit to anything. Move to the cheese stalls and ask for tastes — this is expected, not pushy. The raw bar vendors are usually midway through the building and are the natural midpoint break: order oysters or a tostada, eat standing, and watch the market work around you. After the raw bar, work toward the back wall where the cooked food counters concentrate — chilaquiles, tacos, and the exotic meat preparations if you want to experiment. Finish at the specialty importers near the far wall, which carry Japanese sake, Spanish paprika, French mustard, and quality olive oils that are genuinely hard to find at competitive prices elsewhere in the city. The full loop with stops takes about 90 minutes and costs around 300–400 pesos if you eat and taste along the way.
The detail that makes San Juan more interesting than just a shopping stop is that it's a working procurement market for the city's restaurant scene. Chefs from restaurants in Polanco, Roma, and Condesa send staff here for ingredients that either don't exist at regular suppliers or are better quality than anything available through conventional channels. The sashimi-grade bluefin and yellowfin tuna — which changes by season — goes to Japanese restaurants across the city. The aged European cheeses supply hotel kitchens and European-style bistros. The huitlacoche (corn fungus, a pre-Hispanic ingredient sometimes called 'Mexican truffle') that appears in season goes to contemporary Mexican restaurants where it gets plated as a luxury product. Understanding this supply chain context changes how you look at the pricing: yes, San Juan costs more than a neighborhood tianguis. But you're buying at the same level as a professional kitchen — the gap between what ends up on a 600-peso tasting menu and what you can buy here at cost is narrower than it looks. You can read more about how Mexico City's food traditions developed across centuries to understand why a market like this emerged in the first place.

I take a brief pause from my usual feast or blast review column to fill do-it-yourselfers in on my favorite sources for great products, both foreign and national. Mexico City food shopping will not disappoint the most discerning gourmand.
**MERCADO SAN JUAN** Calle Ernesto Pugibet, centro Metro Salto de Agua – walk up Calle Lopez and turn left at Delicias (or down Lopez if you are coming from the Alameda – you will see the enormous Telmex tower which is across the street view map
The market is, in theory, open daily until around 5 p.m. but some vendors start packing up earlier – there is free parking for customers next door.
This renowned market has existed in some form since colonial times. Chefs and home cooks alike frequent its aisles in search of the perfect duck, cabrito, or lobster. Exotic fresh produce and fruits are offered as are artisan national and imported cheeses: go to **Gastronomica San Juan**, stall no.162,and its neighbor **La Jersey** – they will let you sample. The nationally produced and excellent goat, cow and sheep cheese, many from the state of Queretaro are much cheaper than the imported ones. These stands, as well as **La Catalana** offer good cold cuts as well.
In the seafood area mussels, clams oysters and calamares (they will clean them on request) are often available fresh as are unusual varieties of fish, fresh tuna and amazing big shrimp either in or out of the shell. Spaniards eyes will pop when they see the hideous but delicious percebes at a fraction of the price of the old country.

See also: The Condesa Tuesday Tianguis, The Polanco Saturday Tianguis

texts.0:
The seafood vendors are freshest before noon, and the market is far less crowded Tuesday through Friday — weekend crowds double the wait at the raw bar counters
Cheese and charcuterie vendors usually accept cards; the cooked food counters often don't — 200–300 pesos in small bills covers a full eat-through visit
Ask specifically for manchego español if you want the sheep's-milk aged version — the domestic manchego sold everywhere else in the city is a completely different product
Mexico City has roughly 300 public markets, and almost all of them follow a similar format: produce, cooked food, clothing, hardware, and household goods in rough equal measure. Mercado de San Juan, which sits on Calle Ernesto Pugibet 21 just south of the Alameda Central in Centro Histórico, took a different path. Over decades, it became the market where the city's specialty importers and gourmet food vendors concentrated — which meant the cheesemongers, the charcutiers, the exotic meat traders, and the sashimi-grade seafood suppliers who also sold to restaurants all ended up here. By the 2000s it had become the go-to source for European cheeses, Iberian charcuterie, wild mushrooms, and ingredients that simply don't exist in regular Mexican supermarkets. The result is an odd, specific place: a functioning neighborhood market with local staples on one end and imported Italian truffle and Japanese sake on the other. The building occupies a full city block, with around 200 vendor stalls organized loosely by category — cheese and charcuterie on one side, seafood and cooked food along the back, produce and specialty dry goods through the middle. It's clean, well-lit, and navigable on a first visit once you walk the full loop.
Located at Calle Ernesto Pugibet 21, Centro Histórico — nearest metro: Salto del Agua (Lines 1 and 8)
Open Monday–Saturday 9 AM–6 PM, Sunday 9 AM–5 PM
Around 200 vendor stalls in a single enclosed building
texts.1:
The cheese selection at San Juan is probably the best you'll find in Mexico City outside of a specialty import shop. Several stalls carry aged Spanish manchego — the real sheep's-milk version produced in La Mancha, not the mild domestic cow's-milk product sold everywhere else under the same name. You'll also find French camembert, Italian parmigiano-reggiano sold by the wedge, cave-aged Roquefort, Dutch gouda in several ages, and Spanish idiazábal. A useful exercise for first-time visitors: ask a vendor to let you taste the imported Spanish manchego next to the Mexican domestic version side by side. The difference — nutty and firm versus mild and rubbery — explains immediately why San Juan exists and why chefs make the trip from Polanco to shop here. The charcuterie stalls carry similar depth: jamón ibérico de bellota sliced to order, bresaola from Italian producers, prosciutto di Parma, and Spanish chorizo ibérico alongside excellent Mexican products including cecina from Yecapixtla (the Morelos town famous for its air-dried beef) and black chorizo from Oaxacan producers. The vendors are patient and accustomed to questions — this is one of the few markets in the city where asking for tastes before buying is normal and expected.
Get short, interactive stories that make each place easier to remember while you travel.
texts.2:
The seafood section runs along one side of the building, and a handful of vendors have built what amounts to a standing raw bar right between the stalls. The format is simple: fresh oysters opened to order, served with limón and hot sauce, eaten standing at a small counter. The oysters come from Baja California (Pacific oysters, briny and clean) or the Gulf of Mexico — ask the vendor which batch is freshest if both are available, since they don't restock at the same frequency. Beyond oysters, the same vendors sell tostadas de atún — raw tuna on a fried corn tostada with avocado, cucumber, and a swipe of mayo — and aguachile de camarón, raw shrimp marinated in lime juice and serrano chile until the acid 'cooks' the protein into something bright and clean-tasting with real heat at the end. The seafood vendors at San Juan source directly from suppliers who also sell to high-end restaurants, which means the quality and freshness track closely to what you'd get at a sit-down restaurant in Roma Norte for significantly less money. Expect to pay around 80–120 pesos for a serving of oysters, 60–80 for a tostada.
Pacific oysters from Baja California: briny and firm — the more reliably consistent option
Tostadas de atún: raw tuna, avocado, cucumber on a fried tostada — the best value item in the market
Aguachile: ask for the spice level before ordering — San Juan versions tend toward serious heat
texts.3:
The exotic meat stalls are the part of Mercado de San Juan that generates the most social media content, and they deserve both the attention and a little context. Yes, you can buy ostrich, crocodile, venison, wild boar, and occasionally lion meat at certain stalls. The vendors are licensed and the products legally sourced from registered farms — this is not a black market situation. The crocodile, which comes from regulated farms in Tabasco and Chiapas, is the most approachable option: the tail meat is lean and firm with a texture somewhere between chicken and a dense white fish, usually served as tacos with salsa verde. It's genuinely good and worth ordering once. Ostrich from Hidalgo farms is served as a steak cut — lower in fat than beef, darker in color, and mild enough that it takes a chile marinade well. The lion meat, when it appears, comes from exotic animal operations and is expensive enough that vendors price it by the gram; the flavor itself is unremarkable — mild and lean — and the price premium is entirely for the novelty. Order the crocodile. Skip the lion unless the story is the whole point for you.
Crocodile: farmed in Tabasco and Chiapas — lean tail meat served as tacos with salsa verde, genuinely worth trying
Ostrich: from Hidalgo farms — steak cut, lower fat than beef, takes seasoning well
Lion: legally sourced, overpriced for what it is — the story costs more than the flavor
texts.4:
San Juan is small enough to cover fully in an hour, but the most satisfying way to visit is to plan around the food counters rather than treating it as a grocery run. Start near the entrance with a slow pass through the produce section — the stacks of dried chiles, heirloom corn varieties, and specialty mushrooms (huitlacoche, morels, chanterelles) give you a sense of the market's range before you commit to anything. Move to the cheese stalls and ask for tastes — this is expected, not pushy. The raw bar vendors are usually midway through the building and are the natural midpoint break: order oysters or a tostada, eat standing, and watch the market work around you. After the raw bar, work toward the back wall where the cooked food counters concentrate — chilaquiles, tacos, and the exotic meat preparations if you want to experiment. Finish at the specialty importers near the far wall, which carry Japanese sake, Spanish paprika, French mustard, and quality olive oils that are genuinely hard to find at competitive prices elsewhere in the city. The full loop with stops takes about 90 minutes and costs around 300–400 pesos if you eat and taste along the way.
The detail that makes San Juan more interesting than just a shopping stop is that it's a working procurement market for the city's restaurant scene. Chefs from restaurants in Polanco, Roma, and Condesa send staff here for ingredients that either don't exist at regular suppliers or are better quality than anything available through conventional channels. The sashimi-grade bluefin and yellowfin tuna — which changes by season — goes to Japanese restaurants across the city. The aged European cheeses supply hotel kitchens and European-style bistros. The huitlacoche (corn fungus, a pre-Hispanic ingredient sometimes called 'Mexican truffle') that appears in season goes to contemporary Mexican restaurants where it gets plated as a luxury product. Understanding this supply chain context changes how you look at the pricing: yes, San Juan costs more than a neighborhood tianguis. But you're buying at the same level as a professional kitchen — the gap between what ends up on a 600-peso tasting menu and what you can buy here at cost is narrower than it looks. You can read more about how Mexico City's food traditions developed across centuries to understand why a market like this emerged in the first place.

San Diego, CA April 6, 2009 -- MexGrocer.com, the nation's leading online grocery store for authentic Mexican food products and ingredients. Contact: Ignacio Hernandez at info@mexgrocer.com, 858-270-0577 Mon-Fri 9am-6pm PT.
**MexGrocer.com is Ready for the Fun of Mexico's Cinco de Mayo**
The ever popular Mexican holiday Cinco de Mayo, the Fifth of May, is just around the corner and excitement is already growing in anticipation of the big and fun day.
Furthermore, the time is now to get ready for the festivities, and MexGrocer.com just the place to order your culturally correct a la Mexicana food, cooking needs and ingredients, beverages, and fiesta favorites.
With a fresh new website look, MexGrocer will help you celebrate Cinco de Mayo, a Mexican holiday that commemorates the victory of Mexican troops over French forces in the May 5, 1862 Battle of Puebla, that ultimately led to the expulsion of the interventionists of Napoleon III in 1867.
Today, San Diego, California based MexGrocer.com has a wide variety of Mexican food, spices, cooking utensils, cookbooks and many other popular products ready for immediate shipment, and we look forward to celebrating not only Cinco de Mayo with you, but every day of the year. MexGrocer.com has been serving Mexican food lovers, cooks at home and small restaurant chefs for the past nine years, customers who live throughout the continental United States as well as in Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. Members of the U.S. armed forces are connoisseurs of fine Mexican food, and orders are sent daily to bases at home and Military Post Offices abroad. As well, the number of customers in Canada is growing.
So, wherever you live please visit us often at https://www.MexGrocer.com, and to everyone – **¡Feliz Cinco de Mayo!**
**MexGrocer.com Opens New Distribution Center in San Diego, California**
**Online grocery store focused on authentic Mexican food and cooking products will now do its own warehousing and order fulfillment.**
San Diego, CA January 23, 2007 -- MexGrocer.com, the nation's leading online grocery store for authentic Mexican food products and ingredients, announces the move of its distribution center to San Diego, California.

"Our distribution Center, for products that include hard-to-find, non-perishable and authentic Mexican food, household products, cooking tips, Mexican recipes and Mexican cookbooks, is now located in San Diego," said MexGrocer.com president Ignacio Hernandez. "This is just one of several important changes we will be implementing in 2007 to provide our consumers with a much better service level and product offering."
The new address for MexGrocer.com LLC is:
4901 Morena Blvd., Suite 1106
San Diego, California 92117
Telephone: 858-270-0577
Website: http://www.mexgrocer.com
MexGrocer.com, which was founded by Ignacio Hernandez and Nacho Hernandez Jr. in 2000, offers more than 1,200 specialty Mexican food products from leading imported and national brands, is today selling and shipping to over 12,000 cities throughout the 50 states in the US.
MexGrocer.com streamlines the shopping process by eliminating the difficulty of having to drive to multiple stores in search of authentic Mexican food products not commonly in stock at conventional grocers. It also provides an expert solution to all chefs looking for authentic Mexican food recipes, as well as Mexican cookbooks in both English and Spanish. This exceptional concept is available at one user-friendly location, offering secure shopping and complemented by rapid and reliable delivery services.
**MexGrocer.com Products Now Available on Amazon.com**
_As Part of the Launch of the Gourmet Food Store on Amazon.com, MexGrocer.com Will Be Providing Its Wide Selection of Mexican food to Customers Nationwide_.
MexGrocer Press Release San Diego, CA, Date November 6, 2003 – MexGrocer.com, the leader in selling authentic Mexican food online, today announced that its products can be found at Amazon.com’s new Gourmet Food store. Amazon.com is an online retailer with 37 million active customer accounts, where customers can find and discover anything they may want to buy online.

Amazon.com’s Gourmet Food store provides customers with the deepest selection across a wide range of foods so that they can discover and try new things as well as find old favorites. By working with Amazon.com, MexGrocer.com streamlines the shopping process by eliminating the difficulty of having to find Mexican food products in multiple online stores and not commonly in stock at conventional grocers (e.g. hot sauces, salsa, chipotle peppers, tamale mix and corn husks).
“This alliance will help us reach a much bigger marketplace for consumers who have an appetite for specialty ethnic foods,” says Ignacio Hernandez, President of MexGrocer.com. “Today we have serviced more than 4,600 cities in all 50 states in the U.S. including Hawaii and Alaska.”
According to Datamonitor, the total Mexican food market was valued at $18.3 billion in 2002. MexGrocer.com believes it will capture a portion of these sales through its e-commerce solution and alliances by filling this niche. They look forward to serving Hispanics, primarily Mexican Americans, as well as other consumers who are cooking enthusiasts and love to try new Mexican food recipes.

# # #
**Online Mexican Grocery Service Proves That Salsa Is Much More Popular Than Ketchup**
San Diego, CA, September 16, 2003 (PR Web)--September 16 is Mexican Independence Day and Ignacio Hernandez and Son, founders of MexGrocer.com have a lot to celebrate. Three years ago, the largest online authentic Mexican food store was launched on Mexican Independence Day and today ranks as the leading online Mexican grocery store in the U.S. “We are the experts in Mexican food cooking and Mexican recipes,” Hernandez says, President of MexGrocer.com adding “Today we have serviced over 4,500 cities in all 50 states in the U.S. including Hawaii and Alaska.” The success of this San Diego, California-based company lies in Hernandez’s 30 years experience in the Mexican food industry and in family tradition going back four generations. Popular brands such as Herdez, Dona Maria, La Victoria, and Embasa were either founded or managed by this successful family.
If frequent trips to Mexico do not fit into your busy schedule, MexGrocer.com is the next best thing. The Hernandez family will take you inside the kitchens and more importantly the pantries of the best and finest in Mexican food cuisine. This valuable resource gives you access to unique but essential cooking products while providing you with experienced culinary instruction without having to navigate through smoky kitchens, taco stands, or travel off the beaten path.
Pinpointing tasty salsas or choosing from the remaining 800 plus items MexGrocer.com offers is an easy and cost-efficient process. Through a partnership with Royal Crown Foods, one of the largest Mexican food distributors in the U.S., items are available and ready for delivery anywhere in the United States. Typically, specialty markets stock 200 items at best. And while you’re at it, MexGrocer.com is a bilingual site so if you would like to brush up on your Spanish or practice your English, there are many pictures to assist you. Remember that Christopher Columbus not only discovered America but showed off the chile pepper to his friends.
MexGrocer.com brings authentic Mexican food to your home.

# # #
MexGrocer.com is the leading online Mexican grocery store in the U.S. headquartered in San Diego, CA. Founders are Ignacio Hernandez & Ignacio Hernandez, Jr. with over 22,000 customers nationwide. MexGrocer.com is celebrating their three year anniversary today, September 16, 2003.
**MexGrocer.com achieves selling hard-to-find Mexican food in more than 4,000 cities nationwide.**
_-- MEXGROCER.COM CAPITALIZES ON THE $18 BILLION MEXICAN FOOD MARKET AND THE GROWTH IN ONLINE GROCERY SHOPPING --_
SAN DIEGO, CA – October 25th, 2002 - After two years in business with continuous growth, MexGrocer.com has won a niche in the online grocery market with its successful business model and authenticity.
MexGrocer.com is focused on selling non-perishable specialty Mexican food products, kitchen utensils, household items, and cookbooks. The company has also built an expanding community by giving its customers free cooking tips, culture articles and the best selection of Mexican recipes on the Internet. They offer the largest assortment of Mexican products at competitive prices due to its alliance with Royal Crown Foods, one of the top Mexican food distributors in the U.S., which allows quick order fulfillment while UPS ensures expedient, reliable delivery of all orders nationwide.
“Today we have serviced over 4,000 cities in all 50 states in the US and Canada,” says Ignacio Hernandez, President of MexGrocer.com. “Our bilingual store is dedicated to enhance our customers shopping experience, allowing them to save time and money by offering all of its favorite Mexican products in one convenient location. We offer over 1,000 different items, where local grocers may only have shelf space for 50 to 100.”
MexGrocer.com streamlines the shopping process by eliminating the difficulty of having to drive to multiple stores in search of authentic Mexican products not commonly in stock at conventional grocers (e.g. molcajete stone bowl, chipotle peppers, tamale mix and corn husks). It also provides an expert solution to cooking enthusiasts looking to make something new with these ingredients.

# # #
According to Datamonitor, the total Mexican food market will be valued at $18.3 billion in 2002. MexGrocer.com, the leading online Mexican grocer, believes it will capture a portion of these sales through its e-commerce solution by filling this niche. The company is targeting middle to upper income Hispanics, primarily Mexican Americans, as well as Anglo consumers who have an appetite for specialty ethnic foods.
Ignacio Hernandez, Founder and President of MexGrocer.com, brings over 30 years experience in the Mexican food industry and the Hispanic Market to this venture. As a senior executive and member of the founding family of HERDEZ, the leading food processor in Mexico with brands such as Herdez, Doña Maria, Bufalo and McCormick, he founded and managed the USA division. Mr. Hernandez then established two important Mexican food businesses in North America. These include popular brands such as Del Fuerte and La Gloria in Mexico, La Victoria and Embasa in the U.S.

# Specialty Food Shop Mexico California Northgate Market
[[](https://www.instagram.com/mortgagesbynikki) mortgagesbynikki 248 We finally made it! We’ve been wanting to check out this market for a while, but we knew it was not going to be your average in and out grocery trip. Most of you know I’m a big foodie, so Northgate’s Mercado González concept is definitely my version of a good time. It’s basically a Mexican food hall and market rolled into one, designed to feel like the traditional mercados in Mexico with more than 20 food stands and pretty much every ingredient you could imagine. Going on a Saturday definitely added to the chaos! We grabbed some tacos dorados to fuel up for shopping and I washed mine down with an agua fresca de mamey. Miché while shopping? Yes please! We watched our churros get fried, picked up tortillas that were literally hot off the press, and wandered the aisles sampling different foods and gathering ingredients for dinner. Mom also wanted to take me to a spot called Fermentation Farm for fresh kombucha. I got myself bottles of my two favorite fruit flavors: guava and passion fruit. I also snagged a fermented sambal that turned into a tangy drizzle for blackened cod and cheesy chile tacos for dinner. I planned this trip home to spend time with my mama and sister with no real agenda. Yesterday was a fun little adventure filled with good food and unhurried wandering, and it was exactly what I needed. What's your favorite cultural market to check out unique eats near you? I'd love some ideas on more places to check out 🙌🏽](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DVobssDkRiH/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

San Diego, CA April 6, 2009 -- MexGrocer.com, the nation's leading online grocery store for authentic Mexican food products and ingredients. Contact: Ignacio Hernandez at info@mexgrocer.com, 858-270-0577 Mon-Fri 9am-6pm PT.
**MexGrocer.com is Ready for the Fun of Mexico's Cinco de Mayo**
The ever popular Mexican holiday Cinco de Mayo, the Fifth of May, is just around the corner and excitement is already growing in anticipation of the big and fun day.
Furthermore, the time is now to get ready for the festivities, and MexGrocer.com just the place to order your culturally correct a la Mexicana food, cooking needs and ingredients, beverages, and fiesta favorites.
With a fresh new website look, MexGrocer will help you celebrate Cinco de Mayo, a Mexican holiday that commemorates the victory of Mexican troops over French forces in the May 5, 1862 Battle of Puebla, that ultimately led to the expulsion of the interventionists of Napoleon III in 1867.
Today, San Diego, California based MexGrocer.com has a wide variety of Mexican food, spices, cooking utensils, cookbooks and many other popular products ready for immediate shipment, and we look forward to celebrating not only Cinco de Mayo with you, but every day of the year. MexGrocer.com has been serving Mexican food lovers, cooks at home and small restaurant chefs for the past nine years, customers who live throughout the continental United States as well as in Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. Members of the U.S. armed forces are connoisseurs of fine Mexican food, and orders are sent daily to bases at home and Military Post Offices abroad. As well, the number of customers in Canada is growing.
So, wherever you live please visit us often at https://www.MexGrocer.com, and to everyone – **¡Feliz Cinco de Mayo!**
**MexGrocer.com Opens New Distribution Center in San Diego, California**
**Online grocery store focused on authentic Mexican food and cooking products will now do its own warehousing and order fulfillment.**
San Diego, CA January 23, 2007 -- MexGrocer.com, the nation's leading online grocery store for authentic Mexican food products and ingredients, announces the move of its distribution center to San Diego, California.
texts.1:
"Our distribution Center, for products that include hard-to-find, non-perishable and authentic Mexican food, household products, cooking tips, Mexican recipes and Mexican cookbooks, is now located in San Diego," said MexGrocer.com president Ignacio Hernandez. "This is just one of several important changes we will be implementing in 2007 to provide our consumers with a much better service level and product offering."
The new address for MexGrocer.com LLC is:
4901 Morena Blvd., Suite 1106
San Diego, California 92117
Telephone: 858-270-0577
Website: http://www.mexgrocer.com
MexGrocer.com, which was founded by Ignacio Hernandez and Nacho Hernandez Jr. in 2000, offers more than 1,200 specialty Mexican food products from leading imported and national brands, is today selling and shipping to over 12,000 cities throughout the 50 states in the US.
MexGrocer.com streamlines the shopping process by eliminating the difficulty of having to drive to multiple stores in search of authentic Mexican food products not commonly in stock at conventional grocers. It also provides an expert solution to all chefs looking for authentic Mexican food recipes, as well as Mexican cookbooks in both English and Spanish. This exceptional concept is available at one user-friendly location, offering secure shopping and complemented by rapid and reliable delivery services.
**MexGrocer.com Products Now Available on Amazon.com**
_As Part of the Launch of the Gourmet Food Store on Amazon.com, MexGrocer.com Will Be Providing Its Wide Selection of Mexican food to Customers Nationwide_.
MexGrocer Press Release San Diego, CA, Date November 6, 2003 – MexGrocer.com, the leader in selling authentic Mexican food online, today announced that its products can be found at Amazon.com’s new Gourmet Food store. Amazon.com is an online retailer with 37 million active customer accounts, where customers can find and discover anything they may want to buy online.
texts.2:
Amazon.com’s Gourmet Food store provides customers with the deepest selection across a wide range of foods so that they can discover and try new things as well as find old favorites. By working with Amazon.com, MexGrocer.com streamlines the shopping process by eliminating the difficulty of having to find Mexican food products in multiple online stores and not commonly in stock at conventional grocers (e.g. hot sauces, salsa, chipotle peppers, tamale mix and corn husks).
“This alliance will help us reach a much bigger marketplace for consumers who have an appetite for specialty ethnic foods,” says Ignacio Hernandez, President of MexGrocer.com. “Today we have serviced more than 4,600 cities in all 50 states in the U.S. including Hawaii and Alaska.”
According to Datamonitor, the total Mexican food market was valued at $18.3 billion in 2002. MexGrocer.com believes it will capture a portion of these sales through its e-commerce solution and alliances by filling this niche. They look forward to serving Hispanics, primarily Mexican Americans, as well as other consumers who are cooking enthusiasts and love to try new Mexican food recipes.

San Diego, CA, September 16, 2003 (PR Web)--September 16 is Mexican Independence Day and Ignacio Hernandez and Son, founders of MexGrocer.com have a lot to celebrate. Three years ago, the largest online authentic Mexican food store was launched on Mexican Independence Day and today ranks as the leading online Mexican grocery store in the U.S. “We are the experts in Mexican food cooking and Mexican recipes,” Hernandez says, President of MexGrocer.com adding “Today we have serviced over 4,500 cities in all 50 states in the U.S. including Hawaii and Alaska.” The success of this San Diego, California-based company lies in Hernandez’s 30 years experience in the Mexican food industry and in family tradition going back four generations. MexGrocer.com brings authentic Mexican food to your home.

Inside Northgate González Market's immersive new 'Mercado'
opened.information:
Source: https://www.grocerydive.com/news/northgate-gonzalez-markets-mercado-store-mexican-cuisine-shook-kelley/700248/
Title: Inside Northgate González Market’s immersive new ‘Mercado’
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
A newly opened store in Costa Mesa, California, aims to flip the traditional grocery shopping experience on its head by immersing consumers in Mexican culture and cuisine.
Mercado González, which opened earlier this month, is a new concept from Northgate González Market that offers up authentic cuisine in food stalls and a Mexican fine-dining restaurant. The store also serves as a celebration of Mexican culture with its vivid and colorful design elements.
Architect Kevin Kelley, whose firm Shook Kelley designed the location, called the recently opened location a “game changer” for the grocery industry.
“The Hispanic/Latin/Mexican market has been underrepresented in terms of grocery stores ... They have never really had the limelight. They have never been celebrated in a big way. They have never really been viewed for the culinary adventure they bring people on,” Kelley said.
Mercado González is aiming to change that with a store that offers “the sights, scents, sounds, and tastes of Mexico,” according to its website.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### **Celebrating a family legacy and Mexican culture**
After a fire destroyed his shoe shop in Jalostotitlán in Jalisco, Mexico, Don Miguel moved to the United States and converted a liquor store into the first Northgate Market, which opened in Anaheim, California, in 1980. The grocery company’s name stems from the combination of the liquor store’s name — Northgate — with the family name.
The chain celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2020. Currently third-generation owned, Northgate has grown to 43 stores, including the newly opened location with the mercado concept.
Initially, the grocery chain focused on the Mexican consumer before broadening its target customer base to non-Mexican Latin and Hispanic shoppers, Kelley said.
By the time the chain started working with Shook Kelley about three years ago, however, its stores had come to look “[more] like a Ralph’s” as the González family sought to model a traditional American supermarket in order to overcome stereotypes surrounding Hispanic grocery stores, Kelley said.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
“They’re very aware that sometimes people look at Mexican food as not as high class or as high culinary and they don’t believe that and they don’t like that view,” Kelley said.
Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Grocery Dive free daily newsletter
But Shook Kelley encouraged the chain to embrace its roots and roll out a new concept that serves up authentic Mexican cuisine as a differentiated approach and competitive advantage — leading to the creation of Mercado González, Kelley said. In Mexico, mercados serve as lively gathering spots that host numerous vendors.
“What would a real Mexican culture grocery store look like — the actual idea of a mercado?” was the driving question behind the mercado concept, Kelley said.
While the Los Angeles area has a large Hispanic and Latino population, Mercado González aims to cater to Mexican consumers as well as the broader population diversity in the area, Kelley said.
“I believe it will attract the non-Mexicans to this concept because of its authenticity, just as much as we all love to go to a genuine sushi house or a genuine Thai restaurant,” Kelley said about the newly opened store.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### Cooking up authenticity
Inside Mercado González, shoppers can find more than two dozen puestos— food stalls — that serve up both dine-in and carry-out options.
“You can eat in a market but you can also take your food home,” Kelley said.
At the various puestos,customers can get different offerings such as tamales, tacos, aguachiles, ceviches, carnitas, fruit bowls and pizza. There’s even a Mexican candy store.
At Churrería El Moro, shoppers can get churros fried to order, while Chiva Torta is serving up carnitas, tacos and tostadas.
The store directory for Mercado González.
Retrieved from Mercado Gonzálezon November 27, 2023
The traditional fresh foods departments of meat, seafood and produce have been transformed into the Carnicería La Preferída, Marisquería El Puerto and Cremería puestos.
Customers can also eat at Maizano,an upscale Mexican restaurant with sit-down dining costing roughly $60 per person, Kelley said. The restaurant focuses on alta cocina — Mexican haute cuisine — with plates from the Mexican states of Yucatán, Puebla and Oaxaca, Eater LA noted.
Platos fuertes — main courses — include dishes like octopus with peanut red mole and Mexican squash,carne asada,and the catch of the day.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
While Shook Kelley studied traditional Mexican mercados for the design elements, Northgate Market tapped its direct sourcing pipeline to Mexico as well as local Los Angeles businesses.
Mexican culture has “a lot of beliefs about what food does for you, how it should be served[and]when it should be eaten that’s kind of lacking in American food,” Kelley said.
To further build its reputation as an authentic food experience, Mercado González also includes community kitchens that people can use as test or incubator kitchens to help build their food trucks or food businesses, Kelley said.
“It is going to be one of the hottest concepts in the United States … It gets rid of the traditional aisles and rows and perimeter and builds a whole different experience that you cannot get online,” Kelley said.
Three puestos inside of the store.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### Bucking industry norms
Along with its focus on celebrating authentic Mexican cuisine, Mercado González is also standing out from other grocery stores by breaking long-held industry guidelines and standards.
Straying from the simplified design approach at most grocery stores, the new location is bursting with visual panache, Kelley said.
For example,while most stores use two or three fonts in their signage, Mercado González uses more than 80, he said, adding that there are hundreds of different types of signs and dozens of decorative lamp fixtures.
The store uses 210 paint colors, features 115 custom illustrations and nearly 50 types of tiles and more. The 11 murals do more than add an artistic touch — they also tell symbolic and iconic stories relaying Mexican rituals and traditions based on food, Kelley said.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
“It’s the complete opposite of what the industry would [normally] do,” Kelley said.
While Kelley has heard comparisons of the new store to other foodservice-focused players like Wegmans and Eataly, he likened Mercado González more to a farmers market with its authenticity of operators and emphasis on everyday rather than special occasion.
“It’s unlike anything I think the grocery industry has seen,” Kelley said.

Source: https://marveleslie.substack.com/p/13-mexico-city-food-souvenirs
Title: 13 Mexico City Food Souvenirs to Bring Back to Your Kitchen (and One to Skip)
Chunks: 3,4,5,6
I’ve seen many Mexican recipes call for Mexican oregano, but I’ve never gone out of my way to get it. I learned last summer that Mexican oregano is actually very unique from the more common Mediterranean oregano. Mexican oregano is in the lemon verbena family and is more citrusy, pungent, and earthy. I used to think that Mediterranean oregano was a fine substitute for Mexican oregano, but after smelling them side-by-side, I have a very different opinion!
**How to use it**: In a variety of ways, such as in salsas, chilis, marinades, and stews.
**Tips for buying:** I bought some from a vendor in Mercado Medellín, where I was able to ask the vendor for just 50 grams. I’m quite sure you could buy it at any mercado or supermarket.
5.   **Various Dried Chiles (in order from least to most spicy)**
_For reference, a jalapeño is 2500-8000 SHU._
1.   **Ancho** — 1,000–2,000 SHU. Dried poblano, very mild, rich and fruity

    2.   **Pasilla** — 1,000–2,500 SHU. Similar to ancho, earthy and mild with slight fruitiness

    3.   **Cascabel** — 1,500–2,500 SHU. Mild-medium, nutty and smoky

    4.   **Guajillo** — 2,500–5,000 SHU. Mild-medium, tangy and slightly berry-like

    5.   **Morita** — 2,500–8,000 SHU. A smoked jalapeño (like chipotle but smoked less and made with red jalapeños), medium heat with slightly fruity, smoky flavor

    6.   **Arbol** — 15,000–30,000 SHU. Thin and bright with sharp heat
Ancho, Pasilla, Cascabel, Guajillo, Morita, Arbol

It’s pretty common to see dried chiles in the international aisle of big chain grocery stores in the US. In fact, I’ve used some dried chilies in this Sweet Potato Atom.
However, I don’t often see the same variety and quality of chiles here that I found in Mexico. During my trip, I tried so many unbelievably delicious salsas, and I learned that dried chiles are a crucial ingredient in many of them. So, I purchased a few of the mostly commonly used ones. There are even more chile varieties that I didn’t get!
**How to use it**: So many ways! Aside from salsas, I learned that dried peppers are used for moles, stews, soups, adobo, and marinades, and more.
Check out this fantastic Guide to Chiles Used in Salsa Making Course from Douglas | Inspired by México
These are some recipes I’m eyeing:
Chile Morita Salsa Recipe - by Douglas | Inspired by México,
Pozole Rojo Recipe - Isabel Eats
Guajillo Chile Salsa - Pati Jinich
Chile Pasilla Oaxaqueño Salsa - Muy Bueno
Cascabel Taquera Sauce, a Mexican Favorite - Adriana’s Best Recipes
How to make Chile de Arbol Salsa Recipe │Mexican Food Recipes
**Tips for buying:** I got all of these from two different vendors in Mercado Medellín. It’s best to look for peppers with shiny skin and a pliable texture. If they look dusty, dull, and crack easily when bent, then they’re likely old and lack flavor. When I saw some nice-looking chiles, I asked the vendor if I could touch one, and they told me to go for it. You can also find some of these chiles at grocery stores.
6.   **“Burnt Milk” or Goat’s Milk Jam -**_**Cajeta**_**(**_**Cajeta Quemada de leche de cabra)**_

I first heard about cajeta on Substack last year, and I was eager to try it in Mexico City. Cajeta is a milk jam made with goat’s milk. Some people compare it to dulce de leche, but I think it’s quite different. First, goat’s milk has a distinct tangy flavor, which comes through in the cajeta. Second, the cajeta I saw tends to be thinner than dulce de leche. While in Mexico, I tried a few flans that were made with cajeta and I loved the distinct, caramelized, but not-too-sweet flavor they had.
**How to use it**: On top of pancakes, ice cream, in flan de cajeta (this recipe looks good!), and even stirred into coffee.
**Tips for buying**: I bought the most standard grocery store cajeta because I was curious to try it. I saw some more artisanal cajetas in specialty shops like The Green Corner. You can make cajeta yourself, too! This recipe looks good.
7.   **Oreos with the flavor of “Burnt Milk” -**_**Oreo Sabor a Cajeta Quemada**_
I’m a sucker for special edition Oreos, and especially for ones that are regional or country-specific! So, when I saw this Oreo flavor, I HAD to try it. The filling had a very rich, deep flavor that is not exactly what I’d call cajeta flavor (there was no tang). Still, I quite enjoyed it, but Bulut passed on having a second one. More for me. 🙂
**How to use it**: Eat it! Dip it in milk, crumble on top of ice cream or yogurt. Use it any way you’d use a regular Oreo.
**Tips for buying**: I found these in supermarkets like Walmart Express and Sumesa. You might find them at convenience stores like OXXO, too.
8.   **Dried Hibiscus (Dried Roselle) -**_**Flor de**_ _**Jamaica**_
I am sad, borderline distraught, that I did not know about the wonderful world of agua frescas until the ripe age of 31.
Agua frescas are a refreshing beverage, often made by blending fruit, sugar, and lime juice. Sometimes they’re made with other things. Horchata, for instance, is an agua fresca made with rice, milk, and cinnamon.

On this trip, I tried jamaica (hibiscus) agua fresca, and it mildly changed my life. SO DELICIOUS! And so beautiful, too. It’s made by steeping dried hibiscus flowers in boiling water and then straining it, mixing with as much sugar as you prefer, and diluting with more water. It’s berry-like, slightly floral, and somewhere between an iced tea and fruit juice, but I still think I’m underselling it.
**How to use it**: Make agua de jamaica! I’m going to follow this recipe (cut in half or maybe a quarter). It seems quite easy to make! This other recipe includes some warm spices, which sounds like it would add wonderful depth and dimension.
I also saw hibiscus and strawberry jam in one supermarket. I might try to recreate that at home one day, but it seems like I’d need to buy some pectin first, and I’m not sure I want to begin a journey of making homemade jam while I live in NYC.
**Tips for buying**: You can find flor de jamaica at most places—mercados, supermarkets, and bulk food stores. I was in a pinch to buy some right before I left so I got some from Walmart Express. If you are buying from a mercado, you might want to ask for Mexican-grown jamaica, as I came across some that was imported.
9.   **Puffed Amaranth -**_**Amaranto Inflado**_
Amaranth reminds me of quinoa, but with a gentler flavor. In fact, I just look it up, and it’s quite similar to quinoa because it’s also a gluten-free ancient “pseudocereal.” In other words, it’s a seed used like a grain. It’s a good source of protein and fiber, too. Amaranth is native to Central America so it makes sense why it was quite abundant in Mexico City. The version I bought is air-puffed amaranth, which can be eaten as-is (without boiling). It tastes slightly nutty and has a light, crispy texture.
**How to use it:** Most commonly, puffed amaranth is eaten like cereal. I plan to use it to make granola (along with oats and other seeds). I wonder if it could be used to make “rice” crispy treats, too.
