opened.information:
Source: https://www.travelawaits.com/2668531/food-shopping-in-mexico-vs-the-us/
Title: 7 Ways Food Shopping In Mexico Is Different From The U.S., And Why I Like It Better
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
Ever since I learned to cook in my 20s, when I lived in Vancouver, British Columbia, and bought groceries at the Chinese greengrocer down the street, I’ve found foraging for food one of life’s sensory pleasures. Nowadays, I shop primarily in the two towns where I divide my life: Eureka, on California’s North Coast, and Guanajuato, a UNESCO World Heritage site in central Mexico, where I find the process especially pleasurable. Here are seven ways food shopping is different in the two cultures.
Kettle Moraine North - Mauthe Lake Recreation Area
Mercado Hidalgo (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)

## 1. Getting There
I’m a walker, and I love doing errands on foot. This is easy in Guanajuato because the streets in _el centro_, where our house is located, are pedestrianized, colorful, and lively. Since the places where I buy food are only a few minutes away, I shop most days of the week. Everything is nearby, so it doesn’t matter if I forget something.
The main place I shop is a small grocery store three minutes from our home called Ahorrema$_*_ (which translates to Save More — and the Mexican symbol for the peso is the same as the symbol for the U.S. dollar). If I can’t find what I want there, I go to a similar shop another five minutes away. The city also has two chain supermarkets, Soriana and La Comer, which I reach by walking through one of Guanajuato’s famous tunnels. I also occasionally shop at the Mercado Hidalgo, with its beautiful clock tower on the rooftop, designed by Eiffel, of Eiffel Tower fame.
No matter where I’ve lived in the U.S., on the other hand, it has never been simple to go food shopping on foot. In Eureka, I’m happy that my favorite economy supermarket, Grocery Outlet, is only a 10-minute walk from our home in historic Old Town, a neighborhood studded with Victorian mansions. Unfortunately, the only way to get there is by crossing Fourth and Fifth Streets, also known as 101, the north-south U.S. highway that cuts right through the city. These six-lane, fast-moving thoroughfares are busy with cars, buses, pick-ups, RVs, and even logging trucks. Walking to buy food in Eureka simply doesn’t offer the same sensory pleasure as it does in Mexico.
WinCo (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
In Eureka, I also shop at WinCo, a large chain supermarket about 10 minutes away by car. WinCo is neither aesthetic or hip, but it offers a wide selection, it’s unpretentious, and the staff is friendly.

## 2. Mom-And-Pop Stores
Mexico is a country where small businesses still thrive despite the inroads of the nationwide convenience store, OXXO, and big-box stores like Walmart and Costco. While many expats belong to Costco, a half-hour drive away, we aren’t motivated to be members since we don’t have a car and we don’t buy food in large quantities. Our Mexican fridge is smaller than the standard U.S. type, and we don’t have a separate freezer.
Ahorrema$ has much of what we need. It consists of three narrow aisles packed with fruits and vegetables, canned foods, snacks, condiments, meat, and dairy. I also shop at a health food store minutes from our house, where I buy homemade granola, basmati rice, chili-garlic sauce, hoisin sauce, miso, and delicious ginger cookies.

## 3. Just One!
At Ahorrema$_,_ eggs are sold in bulk, so I can ask the employee behind the meat and dairy counter to bag just one egg if I wish. I can also buy just one stick of butter for the _bolillo_ (roll) that we like with soup. As is common in Europe, in Mexico, we buy freshly baked _bolillos_ at a dedicated bakery,the _panadería,_ not at a general grocery.
Since Barry and I don’t eat much dairy, buying just one or two eggs at a time and one stick of butter is brilliant. Ahorrema$ also sells small store-bagged dried fruits and spices like oregano, thyme, ginger, cumin, and sesame seeds at much lower prices than at the supermarket.
Fruteria (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)

## 4. Fruterías
Unlike what they sound like, _fruterías_ sell not only fruit but also vegetables. I love buying mangos, papayas, mandarins, and prickly-skinned tunas (a sweet pear-like fruit, not fish) to make fruit salads and smoothies. Because these fruits are native to Mexico, they taste especially sweet and juicy. I buy less fruit in the U.S. because I find it bland.
Condiment section (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)

## 5. Availability And Selection
There’s definitely more selection in the U.S. — sometimes to the point that it’s overwhelming. In a typical American supermarket, for example, you’ll see a huge range of peanut butters: crunchy, creamy, low-fat, organic, natural, unsweetened, unsalted, and so on. In Mexico, you’re likely to find just one brand of plain peanut butter. The same is true of many other goods. You won’t find tomato sauce in six flavors.
That said, the availability of foods in Mexico has increased so much in the last 20 years that there’s little I miss from the U.S. Unlike in 1999, when we first visited Guanajuato, I can now buy brussels sprouts, leeks, spinach, parmesan, blue cheese, feta, balsamic vinegar, coconut milk, hummus, and many Asian condiments. Both La Comer and Soriana now offer “Gourmet” sections, where vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, and international foods are sold.
Availability, though, can be very hit and miss. If I like a product in a Guanajuato store, I’ve learned to buy more than one of it because it may not be in stock the next time I visit.
There are a couple of foods I wish I could get in Mexico. At WinCo, I buy a packaged soup called Organic Roasted Red Pepper & Tomato, sold in a box — great for a fast lunch when I don’t feel like cooking. I love Tasty Bite Indian packaged foods, too, but I’m not going to schlep either of these to Mexico! We do bring down small, lightweight items that are either unavailable or more expensive in Mexico, like our favorite teas, vitamins, ibuprofen, and sunscreen.

## 6. Prices
Since Barry and I are not meat eaters, we don’t spend a lot of money on food in either country. Still, we save money in Mexico, where most produce costs 50 to 60 percent less than in the U.S. Imported products often cost more but are still easily affordable for expats — less so to Mexicans, who are vulnerable to the current rate of exchange.
Meat and cheese section (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)

## 7. Speaking Spanish
Shopping offers me the perfect opportunity to talk with locals.I buy bulk Chiapas coffee at a café a few minutes away, where I chat with the barista, Francisco, while he grinds the coffee. And at the liquor store where I buy wine, I talk with Nico or Pati, who know my favorite brand, Don Simon. The last time I was there, they invited me to join them in the back for a tumbler of tequila, and we chatted for an hour.
I like food shopping so much, I’d probably enjoy buying groceries on the moon. Any time, anywhere. But in Mexico, it’s especially easy, fun, and personable — a whole-body experience that lifts my spirits.
_Editor’s Note: For more on Louisa’s adventures, consider her take on Pueblos Magicos and how to explore the magical small towns of Mexico, the 10 reasons she and her husband prefer a camper van to an RV, and her tips for keeping a memorable travel journal._

# Visiting the FANCIEST grocery store in Mexico
## 54 Comments
### @pablovi77

texts.3:
I’ve seen many Mexican recipes call for Mexican oregano, but I’ve never gone out of my way to get it. I learned last summer that Mexican oregano is actually very unique from the more common Mediterranean oregano. Mexican oregano is in the lemon verbena family and is more citrusy, pungent, and earthy. I used to think that Mediterranean oregano was a fine substitute for Mexican oregano, but after smelling them side-by-side, I have a very different opinion!
**How to use it**: In a variety of ways, such as in salsas, chilis, marinades, and stews.
**Tips for buying:** I bought some from a vendor in Mercado Medellín, where I was able to ask the vendor for just 50 grams. I’m quite sure you could buy it at any mercado or supermarket.
5.   **Various Dried Chiles (in order from least to most spicy)**
_For reference, a jalapeño is 2500-8000 SHU._
1.   **Ancho** — 1,000–2,000 SHU. Dried poblano, very mild, rich and fruity

    2.   **Pasilla** — 1,000–2,500 SHU. Similar to ancho, earthy and mild with slight fruitiness

    3.   **Cascabel** — 1,500–2,500 SHU. Mild-medium, nutty and smoky

    4.   **Guajillo** — 2,500–5,000 SHU. Mild-medium, tangy and slightly berry-like

    5.   **Morita** — 2,500–8,000 SHU. A smoked jalapeño (like chipotle but smoked less and made with red jalapeños), medium heat with slightly fruity, smoky flavor

    6.   **Arbol** — 15,000–30,000 SHU. Thin and bright with sharp heat
Ancho, Pasilla, Cascabel, Guajillo, Morita, Arbol
texts.4:
It’s pretty common to see dried chiles in the international aisle of big chain grocery stores in the US. In fact, I’ve used some dried chilies in this Sweet Potato Atom.
However, I don’t often see the same variety and quality of chiles here that I found in Mexico. During my trip, I tried so many unbelievably delicious salsas, and I learned that dried chiles are a crucial ingredient in many of them. So, I purchased a few of the mostly commonly used ones. There are even more chile varieties that I didn’t get!
**How to use it**: So many ways! Aside from salsas, I learned that dried peppers are used for moles, stews, soups, adobo, and marinades, and more.
Check out this fantastic Guide to Chiles Used in Salsa Making Course from Douglas | Inspired by México
These are some recipes I’m eyeing:
Chile Morita Salsa Recipe - by Douglas | Inspired by México,
Pozole Rojo Recipe - Isabel Eats
Guajillo Chile Salsa - Pati Jinich
Chile Pasilla Oaxaqueño Salsa - Muy Bueno
Cascabel Taquera Sauce, a Mexican Favorite - Adriana’s Best Recipes
How to make Chile de Arbol Salsa Recipe │Mexican Food Recipes
**Tips for buying:** I got all of these from two different vendors in Mercado Medellín. It’s best to look for peppers with shiny skin and a pliable texture. If they look dusty, dull, and crack easily when bent, then they’re likely old and lack flavor. When I saw some nice-looking chiles, I asked the vendor if I could touch one, and they told me to go for it. You can also find some of these chiles at grocery stores.
6.   **“Burnt Milk” or Goat’s Milk Jam -**_**Cajeta**_**(**_**Cajeta Quemada de leche de cabra)**_
texts.5:
I first heard about cajeta on Substack last year, and I was eager to try it in Mexico City. Cajeta is a milk jam made with goat’s milk. Some people compare it to dulce de leche, but I think it’s quite different. First, goat’s milk has a distinct tangy flavor, which comes through in the cajeta. Second, the cajeta I saw tends to be thinner than dulce de leche. While in Mexico, I tried a few flans that were made with cajeta and I loved the distinct, caramelized, but not-too-sweet flavor they had.
**How to use it**: On top of pancakes, ice cream, in flan de cajeta (this recipe looks good!), and even stirred into coffee.
**Tips for buying**: I bought the most standard grocery store cajeta because I was curious to try it. I saw some more artisanal cajetas in specialty shops like The Green Corner. You can make cajeta yourself, too! This recipe looks good.
7.   **Oreos with the flavor of “Burnt Milk” -**_**Oreo Sabor a Cajeta Quemada**_
I’m a sucker for special edition Oreos, and especially for ones that are regional or country-specific! So, when I saw this Oreo flavor, I HAD to try it. The filling had a very rich, deep flavor that is not exactly what I’d call cajeta flavor (there was no tang). Still, I quite enjoyed it, but Bulut passed on having a second one. More for me. 🙂
**How to use it**: Eat it! Dip it in milk, crumble on top of ice cream or yogurt. Use it any way you’d use a regular Oreo.
**Tips for buying**: I found these in supermarkets like Walmart Express and Sumesa. You might find them at convenience stores like OXXO, too.
8.   **Dried Hibiscus (Dried Roselle) -**_**Flor de**_ _**Jamaica**_
I am sad, borderline distraught, that I did not know about the wonderful world of agua frescas until the ripe age of 31.
Agua frescas are a refreshing beverage, often made by blending fruit, sugar, and lime juice. Sometimes they’re made with other things. Horchata, for instance, is an agua fresca made with rice, milk, and cinnamon.
texts.6:
On this trip, I tried jamaica (hibiscus) agua fresca, and it mildly changed my life. SO DELICIOUS! And so beautiful, too. It’s made by steeping dried hibiscus flowers in boiling water and then straining it, mixing with as much sugar as you prefer, and diluting with more water. It’s berry-like, slightly floral, and somewhere between an iced tea and fruit juice, but I still think I’m underselling it.
**How to use it**: Make agua de jamaica! I’m going to follow this recipe (cut in half or maybe a quarter). It seems quite easy to make! This other recipe includes some warm spices, which sounds like it would add wonderful depth and dimension.
I also saw hibiscus and strawberry jam in one supermarket. I might try to recreate that at home one day, but it seems like I’d need to buy some pectin first, and I’m not sure I want to begin a journey of making homemade jam while I live in NYC.
**Tips for buying**: You can find flor de jamaica at most places—mercados, supermarkets, and bulk food stores. I was in a pinch to buy some right before I left so I got some from Walmart Express. If you are buying from a mercado, you might want to ask for Mexican-grown jamaica, as I came across some that was imported.
9.   **Puffed Amaranth -**_**Amaranto Inflado**_
Amaranth reminds me of quinoa, but with a gentler flavor. In fact, I just look it up, and it’s quite similar to quinoa because it’s also a gluten-free ancient “pseudocereal.” In other words, it’s a seed used like a grain. It’s a good source of protein and fiber, too. Amaranth is native to Central America so it makes sense why it was quite abundant in Mexico City. The version I bought is air-puffed amaranth, which can be eaten as-is (without boiling). It tastes slightly nutty and has a light, crispy texture.
**How to use it:** Most commonly, puffed amaranth is eaten like cereal. I plan to use it to make granola (along with oats and other seeds). I wonder if it could be used to make “rice” crispy treats, too.

texts.0:
Ever since I learned to cook in my 20s, when I lived in Vancouver, British Columbia, and bought groceries at the Chinese greengrocer down the street, I’ve found foraging for food one of life’s sensory pleasures. Nowadays, I shop primarily in the two towns where I divide my life: Eureka, on California’s North Coast, and Guanajuato, a UNESCO World Heritage site in central Mexico, where I find the process especially pleasurable. Here are seven ways food shopping is different in the two cultures.
Kettle Moraine North - Mauthe Lake Recreation Area
Mercado Hidalgo (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
texts.1:
## 1. Getting There
I’m a walker, and I love doing errands on foot. This is easy in Guanajuato because the streets in _el centro_, where our house is located, are pedestrianized, colorful, and lively. Since the places where I buy food are only a few minutes away, I shop most days of the week. Everything is nearby, so it doesn’t matter if I forget something.
The main place I shop is a small grocery store three minutes from our home called Ahorrema$_*_ (which translates to Save More — and the Mexican symbol for the peso is the same as the symbol for the U.S. dollar). If I can’t find what I want there, I go to a similar shop another five minutes away. The city also has two chain supermarkets, Soriana and La Comer, which I reach by walking through one of Guanajuato’s famous tunnels. I also occasionally shop at the Mercado Hidalgo, with its beautiful clock tower on the rooftop, designed by Eiffel, of Eiffel Tower fame.
No matter where I’ve lived in the U.S., on the other hand, it has never been simple to go food shopping on foot. In Eureka, I’m happy that my favorite economy supermarket, Grocery Outlet, is only a 10-minute walk from our home in historic Old Town, a neighborhood studded with Victorian mansions. Unfortunately, the only way to get there is by crossing Fourth and Fifth Streets, also known as 101, the north-south U.S. highway that cuts right through the city. These six-lane, fast-moving thoroughfares are busy with cars, buses, pick-ups, RVs, and even logging trucks. Walking to buy food in Eureka simply doesn’t offer the same sensory pleasure as it does in Mexico.
WinCo (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
In Eureka, I also shop at WinCo, a large chain supermarket about 10 minutes away by car. WinCo is neither aesthetic or hip, but it offers a wide selection, it’s unpretentious, and the staff is friendly.
texts.2:
## 2. Mom-And-Pop Stores
Mexico is a country where small businesses still thrive despite the inroads of the nationwide convenience store, OXXO, and big-box stores like Walmart and Costco. While many expats belong to Costco, a half-hour drive away, we aren’t motivated to be members since we don’t have a car and we don’t buy food in large quantities. Our Mexican fridge is smaller than the standard U.S. type, and we don’t have a separate freezer.
Ahorrema$ has much of what we need. It consists of three narrow aisles packed with fruits and vegetables, canned foods, snacks, condiments, meat, and dairy. I also shop at a health food store minutes from our house, where I buy homemade granola, basmati rice, chili-garlic sauce, hoisin sauce, miso, and delicious ginger cookies.
texts.3:
## 3. Just One!
At Ahorrema$_,_ eggs are sold in bulk, so I can ask the employee behind the meat and dairy counter to bag just one egg if I wish. I can also buy just one stick of butter for the _bolillo_ (roll) that we like with soup. As is common in Europe, in Mexico, we buy freshly baked _bolillos_ at a dedicated bakery,the _panadería,_ not at a general grocery.
Since Barry and I don’t eat much dairy, buying just one or two eggs at a time and one stick of butter is brilliant. Ahorrema$ also sells small store-bagged dried fruits and spices like oregano, thyme, ginger, cumin, and sesame seeds at much lower prices than at the supermarket.
Fruteria (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
texts.4:
## 4. Fruterías
Unlike what they sound like, _fruterías_ sell not only fruit but also vegetables. I love buying mangos, papayas, mandarins, and prickly-skinned tunas (a sweet pear-like fruit, not fish) to make fruit salads and smoothies. Because these fruits are native to Mexico, they taste especially sweet and juicy. I buy less fruit in the U.S. because I find it bland.
Condiment section (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
texts.5:
## 5. Availability And Selection
There’s definitely more selection in the U.S. — sometimes to the point that it’s overwhelming. In a typical American supermarket, for example, you’ll see a huge range of peanut butters: crunchy, creamy, low-fat, organic, natural, unsweetened, unsalted, and so on. In Mexico, you’re likely to find just one brand of plain peanut butter. The same is true of many other goods. You won’t find tomato sauce in six flavors.
That said, the availability of foods in Mexico has increased so much in the last 20 years that there’s little I miss from the U.S. Unlike in 1999, when we first visited Guanajuato, I can now buy brussels sprouts, leeks, spinach, parmesan, blue cheese, feta, balsamic vinegar, coconut milk, hummus, and many Asian condiments. Both La Comer and Soriana now offer “Gourmet” sections, where vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free, and international foods are sold.
Availability, though, can be very hit and miss. If I like a product in a Guanajuato store, I’ve learned to buy more than one of it because it may not be in stock the next time I visit.
There are a couple of foods I wish I could get in Mexico. At WinCo, I buy a packaged soup called Organic Roasted Red Pepper & Tomato, sold in a box — great for a fast lunch when I don’t feel like cooking. I love Tasty Bite Indian packaged foods, too, but I’m not going to schlep either of these to Mexico! We do bring down small, lightweight items that are either unavailable or more expensive in Mexico, like our favorite teas, vitamins, ibuprofen, and sunscreen.
texts.6:
## 6. Prices
Since Barry and I are not meat eaters, we don’t spend a lot of money on food in either country. Still, we save money in Mexico, where most produce costs 50 to 60 percent less than in the U.S. Imported products often cost more but are still easily affordable for expats — less so to Mexicans, who are vulnerable to the current rate of exchange.
Meat and cheese section (Photo Credit: Louisa Rogers)
texts.7:
## 7. Speaking Spanish
Shopping offers me the perfect opportunity to talk with locals.I buy bulk Chiapas coffee at a café a few minutes away, where I chat with the barista, Francisco, while he grinds the coffee. And at the liquor store where I buy wine, I talk with Nico or Pati, who know my favorite brand, Don Simon. The last time I was there, they invited me to join them in the back for a tumbler of tequila, and we chatted for an hour.
I like food shopping so much, I’d probably enjoy buying groceries on the moon. Any time, anywhere. But in Mexico, it’s especially easy, fun, and personable — a whole-body experience that lifts my spirits.
_Editor’s Note: For more on Louisa’s adventures, consider her take on Pueblos Magicos and how to explore the magical small towns of Mexico, the 10 reasons she and her husband prefer a camper van to an RV, and her tips for keeping a memorable travel journal._

# Our Heritage - Northgate Market
## Our Heritage


# Our Heritage - Northgate Market
## A dream of
prosperity
One man’s dream and determination turns into a legacy that thrives through the changing of times and passed down to future generations. The González family offers you a look into their heritage and history.

# Humble
beginnings
Hailing from Jalostotitlán, Jalisco, Mexico, Don Miguel González Jiménez was a product of humble beginings. Don Miguel worked as a shoemaker in a small shop in his beloved town.

# purpose found in tragedy
In 1952, after a tragic fire consumed his shoe shop, what was once the pride of Don Miguel resulted in ashes. However, with the support of a loving and caring wife (Doña Teresa Reynoso de González) and with the backing of his community, Don Miguel found comfort and hope.

# motivated by love of family
After a long 14 years of struggle and uncertainty, Don Miguel would make the decision to venture to the United States in order to pursue a better life for his wife and children. The “American Dream” was his path forward.

# a new land for a new start
Years later Don Miguel became a business owner once again, as in 1980 he opened the first ever Northgate Market. Converting a once liquor store into a grocery store was no easy task, but Don Miguel and the rest of his family were no strangers to challenges. Eventually one store, turned into two, and the González family never looked back.

# a foundation for generations
The González family continues to grow as does the history of Northgate Market. The foundation created by Don Miguel and the continued care by the family thereafter, the future is bright for Northgate Market.

# a foundation for generations
### A Culture To Be Proud Of
The González family has built a foundation for Northgate associates to find satisfaction in their work and ulitmately to discover the path to success. Click below to learn more about the culture and values that make up the Northgate Market experience.

opened.information:
Source: https://www.grocerydive.com/news/northgate-gonzalez-markets-mercado-store-mexican-cuisine-shook-kelley/700248/
Title: Inside Northgate González Market’s immersive new ‘Mercado’
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
A newly opened store in Costa Mesa, California, aims to flip the traditional grocery shopping experience on its head by immersing consumers in Mexican culture and cuisine.
Mercado González, which opened earlier this month, is a new concept from Northgate González Market that offers up authentic cuisine in food stalls and a Mexican fine-dining restaurant. The store also serves as a celebration of Mexican culture with its vivid and colorful design elements.
Architect Kevin Kelley, whose firm Shook Kelley designed the location, called the recently opened location a “game changer” for the grocery industry.
“The Hispanic/Latin/Mexican market has been underrepresented in terms of grocery stores ... They have never really had the limelight. They have never been celebrated in a big way. They have never really been viewed for the culinary adventure they bring people on,” Kelley said.
Mercado González is aiming to change that with a store that offers “the sights, scents, sounds, and tastes of Mexico,” according to its website.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### **Celebrating a family legacy and Mexican culture**
After a fire destroyed his shoe shop in Jalostotitlán in Jalisco, Mexico, Don Miguel moved to the United States and converted a liquor store into the first Northgate Market, which opened in Anaheim, California, in 1980. The grocery company’s name stems from the combination of the liquor store’s name — Northgate — with the family name.
The chain celebrated its 40th anniversary in 2020. Currently third-generation owned, Northgate has grown to 43 stores, including the newly opened location with the mercado concept.
Initially, the grocery chain focused on the Mexican consumer before broadening its target customer base to non-Mexican Latin and Hispanic shoppers, Kelley said.
By the time the chain started working with Shook Kelley about three years ago, however, its stores had come to look “[more] like a Ralph’s” as the González family sought to model a traditional American supermarket in order to overcome stereotypes surrounding Hispanic grocery stores, Kelley said.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
“They’re very aware that sometimes people look at Mexican food as not as high class or as high culinary and they don’t believe that and they don’t like that view,” Kelley said.
Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Grocery Dive free daily newsletter
But Shook Kelley encouraged the chain to embrace its roots and roll out a new concept that serves up authentic Mexican cuisine as a differentiated approach and competitive advantage — leading to the creation of Mercado González, Kelley said. In Mexico, mercados serve as lively gathering spots that host numerous vendors.
“What would a real Mexican culture grocery store look like — the actual idea of a mercado?” was the driving question behind the mercado concept, Kelley said.
While the Los Angeles area has a large Hispanic and Latino population, Mercado González aims to cater to Mexican consumers as well as the broader population diversity in the area, Kelley said.
“I believe it will attract the non-Mexicans to this concept because of its authenticity, just as much as we all love to go to a genuine sushi house or a genuine Thai restaurant,” Kelley said about the newly opened store.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### Cooking up authenticity
Inside Mercado González, shoppers can find more than two dozen puestos— food stalls — that serve up both dine-in and carry-out options.
“You can eat in a market but you can also take your food home,” Kelley said.
At the various puestos,customers can get different offerings such as tamales, tacos, aguachiles, ceviches, carnitas, fruit bowls and pizza. There’s even a Mexican candy store.
At Churrería El Moro, shoppers can get churros fried to order, while Chiva Torta is serving up carnitas, tacos and tostadas.
The store directory for Mercado González.
Retrieved from Mercado Gonzálezon November 27, 2023
The traditional fresh foods departments of meat, seafood and produce have been transformed into the Carnicería La Preferída, Marisquería El Puerto and Cremería puestos.
Customers can also eat at Maizano,an upscale Mexican restaurant with sit-down dining costing roughly $60 per person, Kelley said. The restaurant focuses on alta cocina — Mexican haute cuisine — with plates from the Mexican states of Yucatán, Puebla and Oaxaca, Eater LA noted.
Platos fuertes — main courses — include dishes like octopus with peanut red mole and Mexican squash,carne asada,and the catch of the day.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
While Shook Kelley studied traditional Mexican mercados for the design elements, Northgate Market tapped its direct sourcing pipeline to Mexico as well as local Los Angeles businesses.
Mexican culture has “a lot of beliefs about what food does for you, how it should be served[and]when it should be eaten that’s kind of lacking in American food,” Kelley said.
To further build its reputation as an authentic food experience, Mercado González also includes community kitchens that people can use as test or incubator kitchens to help build their food trucks or food businesses, Kelley said.
“It is going to be one of the hottest concepts in the United States … It gets rid of the traditional aisles and rows and perimeter and builds a whole different experience that you cannot get online,” Kelley said.
Three puestos inside of the store.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez

### Bucking industry norms
Along with its focus on celebrating authentic Mexican cuisine, Mercado González is also standing out from other grocery stores by breaking long-held industry guidelines and standards.
Straying from the simplified design approach at most grocery stores, the new location is bursting with visual panache, Kelley said.
For example,while most stores use two or three fonts in their signage, Mercado González uses more than 80, he said, adding that there are hundreds of different types of signs and dozens of decorative lamp fixtures.
The store uses 210 paint colors, features 115 custom illustrations and nearly 50 types of tiles and more. The 11 murals do more than add an artistic touch — they also tell symbolic and iconic stories relaying Mexican rituals and traditions based on food, Kelley said.
Permission granted by Robert Sanchez
“It’s the complete opposite of what the industry would [normally] do,” Kelley said.
While Kelley has heard comparisons of the new store to other foodservice-focused players like Wegmans and Eataly, he likened Mercado González more to a farmers market with its authenticity of operators and emphasis on everyday rather than special occasion.
“It’s unlike anything I think the grocery industry has seen,” Kelley said.

## Our Heritage
texts.7:
# Our Heritage - Northgate Market
## A dream of
prosperity
One man’s dream and determination turns into a legacy that thrives through the changing of times and passed down to future generations. The González family offers you a look into their heritage and history.
texts.8:
# Humble
beginnings
Hailing from Jalostotitlán, Jalisco, Mexico, Don Miguel González Jiménez was a product of humble beginings. Don Miguel worked as a shoemaker in a small shop in his beloved town.
texts.9:
# purpose found in tragedy
In 1952, after a tragic fire consumed his shoe shop, what was once the pride of Don Miguel resulted in ashes. However, with the support of a loving and caring wife (Doña Teresa Reynoso de González) and with the backing of his community, Don Miguel found comfort and hope.
texts.10:
# motivated by love of family
After a long 14 years of struggle and uncertainty, Don Miguel would make the decision to venture to the United States in order to pursue a better life for his wife and children. The “American Dream” was his path forward.
texts.11:
# a new land for a new start
Years later Don Miguel became a business owner once again, as in 1980 he opened the first ever Northgate Market. Converting a once liquor store into a grocery store was no easy task, but Don Miguel and the rest of his family were no strangers to challenges. Eventually one store, turned into two, and the González family never looked back.
texts.12:
# a foundation for generations
The González family continues to grow as does the history of Northgate Market. The foundation created by Don Miguel and the continued care by the family thereafter, the future is bright for Northgate Market.
texts.13:
# a foundation for generations
### A Culture To Be Proud Of
The González family has built a foundation for Northgate associates to find satisfaction in their work and ulitmately to discover the path to success. Click below to learn more about the culture and values that make up the Northgate Market experience.
Learn More
